passage.title: The Mountain That Stores Sunlight
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Across the American South, shiny rows of solar panels soak up bright midday sunshine and turn it into clean power. Yet solar panels face a basic daily problem. They make the most power at noon when the sun sits high in the sky, but families use the most power in the evening when they cook supper and turn on lights. Power lines cannot hold extra power by themselves. Grid crews need giant storage banks to save noon sun for night use.

Some towns put in rooms full of costly shop batteries. However, workers in the North Georgia hills use a much older tool. They use water and the pull of the earth. At Rocky Mountain near Rome, Georgia, two deep lakes sit at two heights on the same ridge. One lake rests in the low valley. The second lake sits in a stone bowl high on the hill. Wide steel tunnels bored straight through the solid rock connect the upper lake to the lower lake.

On sunny days, solar farms make more power than towns need. That is when giant pumps at the dam switch on. Vast gallons of cool river water, drawn from the lower valley lake by reversible electric pumps, are pushed high up the mountain into the upper stone basin. Lifting all that heavy water to the top of the ridge stores energy. It works the same way stretching a rubber band stores a pull. As long as the water stays locked behind the top gates, the power waits safely on the hill.

Soon the sun sinks below the trees. Kitchen lights flick on across the state, and workers open the steel gates. The pull of the earth sends the water roaring back down through the rock tunnels. On its way down, the rushing stream spins huge metal blades called turbines. That spinning motion sends fresh power out to thousands of homes in less than a minute.

Some critics once claimed that pumping water uphill was a waste of effort because the pumps use a small share of power to lift the lake. However, grid planners point out that without storage, extra midday solar power would simply go to waste. By reusing the same water up and down the hill every day, a mountain lake works like a giant rechargeable battery that never wears out.

monsterSentence.verbatimSentence: Vast gallons of cool river water, drawn from the lower valley lake by reversible electric pumps, are pushed high up the mountain into the upper stone basin.
monsterSentence.receiverChunk: Vast gallons of cool river water
distractorChunks: drawn from the lower valley lake
monsterSentence.activeRewrite: Reversible electric pumps draw vast gallons of cool river water from the lower valley lake and push them high up the mountain.

tier2Words.definition: able to run or work in the opposite direction
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root vertere ('to turn') + prefix re- ('back') + suffix -ible ('able to')
tier2Words.contextClue: The same machines pump water up the mountain in the afternoon and spin to make power when water flows back down.

tier2Words.definition: a wide, bowl-shaped hollow in the earth that holds water
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old French bacin, meaning 'a round bowl'
tier2Words.contextClue: The second lake sits in a wide stone bowl high on the mountaintop.

tier2Words.definition: machines with spinning blades that turn moving water or wind into electricity
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin turbo, meaning 'spinning top or whirlwind'
tier2Words.contextClue: On its way down, the rushing stream spins massive metal blades that send fresh power out to homes.

tier2Words.definition: people who point out faults or disagree with a plan
tier2Words.rootHint: From Greek kritikos, meaning 'able to judge'
tier2Words.contextClue: These doubters once claimed that pumping water uphill was a waste of effort, while grid planners disagreed.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Vast gallons of cool river water, drawn from the lower valley lake by reversible electric pumps, are pushed high up the mountain into the upper stone basin."

Based on the structure of the sentence, what draws and pushes the river water, and where does the water end up?

options.text: The upper stone basin pushes the electric pumps down into the lower valley lake.
options.childFeedback: This flips the action upside down! The upper stone basin is just the rock bowl on top of the mountain; it does not push the electric pumps.

options.text: Heavy rain clouds fill the upper stone basin because the valley lake is completely dry.
options.childFeedback: The water comes from the lower valley lake when the electric pumps switch on—not from rain clouds filling a dry lake.

options.text: Cool river water builds the steel tunnels and pushes the mountain into the valley.
options.childFeedback: Workers bored the steel tunnels through the rock in Paragraph 2; river water is what gets pumped through those tunnels up into the basin.

options.text: Reversible electric pumps draw and push the water, and it ends up in the upper stone basin on the mountain.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'drawn... by reversible electric pumps' and 'pushed high up the mountain into the upper stone basin' show that reversible electric pumps draw and push the water into the upper stone basin.

questions.provingSentenceText: Vast gallons of cool river water, drawn from the lower valley lake by reversible electric pumps, are pushed high up the mountain into the upper stone basin.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, 'drawn... by reversible electric pumps' and 'pushed high up the mountain into the upper stone basin' show that reversible electric pumps draw and push the water into the upper stone basin.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'Vast gallons of cool river water' is the subject/receiver, 'reversible electric pumps' is the agent after 'by', and 'into the upper stone basin' is the destination.
questions.retryHint: Look at the 'by' phrase ('by reversible electric pumps') and the 'into' phrase at the end of the sentence in Paragraph 3.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 2 and Paragraph 3:

"One lake rests in the low valley. The second lake sits in a stone bowl high on the hill... Vast gallons of cool river water, drawn from the lower valley lake by reversible electric pumps, are pushed high up the mountain into the upper stone basin."

What does the word basin mean as it is used in Paragraph 3?

options.text: A glass panel that catches midday sunshine
options.childFeedback: Solar panels catch midday sunshine in Paragraph 1, whereas the 'upper stone basin' in Paragraph 3 holds vast gallons of cool river water on the mountain.

options.text: A tall metal tower that holds power lines
options.childFeedback: Power lines are mentioned in Paragraph 1, but you cannot pump vast gallons of river water into a metal power-line tower.

options.text: A bowl-shaped hollow that holds a lake of water
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'basin' means a bowl-shaped hollow that holds a lake of water, which connects directly to the clue in Paragraph 2 that the upper lake 'sits in a stone bowl high on the hill.'

options.text: A narrow underground wire that carries radio signals
options.childFeedback: The passage never mentions radio wires; 'the upper stone basin' is the giant rock bowl on the mountain that holds the upper lake.

questions.provingSentenceText: Vast gallons of cool river water, drawn from the lower valley lake by reversible electric pumps, are pushed high up the mountain into the upper stone basin.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, 'basin' means a bowl-shaped hollow that holds a lake of water, which connects directly to the clue in Paragraph 2 that the upper lake 'sits in a stone bowl high on the hill.'
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 describes the upper lake sitting in 'a stone bowl high on the hill,' which directly defines 'the upper stone basin' in Paragraph 3.
questions.retryHint: Connect 'the upper stone basin' in Paragraph 3 with how Paragraph 2 describes where the second lake sits ('a stone bowl high on the hill').

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 1, why do solar power systems need a way to store energy?

options.text: Solar panels only work during cold winter nights when the wind blows across the hills.
options.childFeedback: Solar panels need sunlight to make electricity—they make the most power at bright midday noon, not on dark winter nights.

options.text: Solar panels make the most power at noon, whereas families use the most electricity in the evening.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 explains the daily mismatch: solar panels make the most power at noon when the sun is high, but families use the most electricity in the evening when cooking supper and turning on lights.

options.text: Power lines automatically store extra electricity for weeks without needing any batteries.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 states the exact opposite: 'Power lines cannot hold extra power by themselves.'

options.text: Engineers in Georgia prefer burning coal at noon instead of turning on solar panels.
options.childFeedback: Coal is never mentioned in the passage; Paragraph 3 explains that sunny days create extra solar power that runs the water pumps.

questions.provingSentenceText: They make the most power at noon when the sun sits high in the sky, but families use the most power in the evening when they cook supper and turn on lights.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 1 explains the daily mismatch: solar panels make the most power at noon when the sun is high, but families use the most electricity in the evening when cooking supper and turning on lights.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 explains the timing mismatch: peak solar production happens at noon, while peak household demand happens in the evening.
questions.retryHint: Read the third sentence of Paragraph 1 to compare when solar panels make the most power versus when families use the most power.

questions.prompt: In Paragraph 5, how do the viewpoints of the critics and the grid planners differ regarding pumped-storage lakes?

options.text: Critics focused on the power used by the pumps, whereas grid planners emphasize that pumping saves extra midday solar power from being wasted.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 contrasts the two views: critics claimed pumping water uphill wasted power, whereas grid planners point out that without storage, extra midday solar power would go completely to waste.

options.text: Critics wanted to build three more lakes on Rocky Mountain, whereas grid planners wanted to drain the valley lake.
options.childFeedback: Neither group suggested building three more lakes or draining the valley; they debated whether pumping water uphill wasted energy or saved extra solar power.

options.text: Both groups agreed that chemical batteries last much longer than stone reservoirs.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 calls shop batteries 'costly,' and Paragraph 5 says the mountain lake works like a giant rechargeable battery that 'never wears out.'

options.text: Grid planners argued that gravity no longer pulls water downhill after sunset.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, gravity ('the pull of the earth') is what sends the water roaring back down through the rock tunnels after sunset.

questions.provingSentenceText: However, grid planners point out that without storage, extra midday solar power would simply go to waste.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 5 contrasts the two views: critics claimed pumping water uphill wasted power, whereas grid planners point out that without storage, extra midday solar power would go completely to waste.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 5 contrasts two perspectives (ELAGSE5RI6): critics saw pumping water uphill as a waste of energy, while grid planners point out that it captures surplus midday solar energy that would otherwise be lost.
questions.retryHint: Compare the first sentence of Paragraph 5 ('Some critics once claimed...') with the second sentence ('However, grid planners point out...').

questions.prompt: Part A: Why does the author compare the Rocky Mountain reservoir system to "a giant rechargeable battery" in Paragraph 5?

options.text: The upper lake is filled with battery acid instead of fresh river water from the valley.
options.childFeedback: The lakes hold 'cool river water'—calling the mountain a rechargeable battery is a comparison for how it stores and releases energy, not literal battery acid.

options.text: It stores extra energy by pumping water uphill during the day and releases that energy by spinning turbines at night, repeating the cycle daily.
options.childFeedback: Like a rechargeable battery, the mountain lake stores extra energy by pumping water uphill during the day and releases that energy by spinning turbines at night, repeating the cycle daily.

options.text: The mountain can only be used once before all the water evaporates into the clouds.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 says the exact opposite: the system reuses the same water up and down the hill every day and 'never wears out.'

options.text: Homeowners can carry buckets of water from the lake to plug into their kitchen lamps.
options.childFeedback: Water cannot be plugged into a lamp! Spinning metal turbines inside the dam's rock tunnels generate electricity that travels through power lines to homes.

questions.provingSentenceText: By reusing the same water up and down the hill every day, a mountain lake works like a giant rechargeable battery that never wears out.
questions.childTip: Like a rechargeable battery, the mountain lake stores extra solar energy during the day (by pumping water uphill) and releases electricity at night (when the water rushes back down to spin turbines), reusing the same water every day.
questions.parentExplanation: Across Paragraphs 3–5, the passage shows that pumping water uphill charges the system with potential energy and letting it rush downhill through turbines discharges electricity, reusing the same water daily like a rechargeable battery.
questions.retryHint: Look at how the mountain reuses the same water in Paragraph 5 to store energy at noon and release power at night.

questions.provingSentenceText: By reusing the same water up and down the hill every day, a mountain lake works like a giant rechargeable battery that never wears out.
questions.childTip: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by explaining that reusing the same water up and down the hill every day makes the mountain lake work like a giant rechargeable battery.
